lessons.title: How Financial Data Is Organized in Oracle Fusion
Business Units, Ledgers and Data Access

slots.practicalActivity: In Oracle's published ERP Cloud table and view documentation (Oracle Help Center's Fusion Applications technical reference for Financials), look up the real documentation entries for one AP_ table, one AR_ table, one GL_ table and one HZ_ table, and for each one record its description, primary key, and two columns the documentation calls out as significant. Then, in your practice environment, open the General Ledger work area and identify your own ledger's assigned business unit(s), writing down the operational boundary (business unit) versus the accounting boundary (the ledger's four Cs: chart of accounts, calendar, currency, convention) you find configured there.
slots.deliverable: A documentation lookup table for one real AP_, AR_, GL_ and HZ_ table (description, primary key, two key columns), plus a written record of your practice ledger's actual four Cs and assigned business unit(s).

slots.practicalActivity: Chapter-ending practice for The Financial Data Model: starting from the business question "which suppliers have invoices open longer than 30 days," name the driving table you'd start from and trace, on paper, the subledger-to-SLA-to-GL path (AP_* -> XLA_* -> GL_*) that question's answer would eventually need to reconcile against. Then look up the real naming-convention rules (the _ALL suffix, the two/three-letter module prefixes) in Oracle's documentation and confirm which prefix and suffix apply to each table you traced.
slots.deliverable: A written subledger-to-GL trace for the 30-days-overdue question, with each table's prefix and _ALL status confirmed against Oracle's own naming-convention documentation.

lessons.title: Customers and the Trading Community Model

slots.practicalActivity: Look up Oracle's real documentation entries for POZ_SUPPLIERS, POZ_SUPPLIER_SITES_ALL_M, HZ_PARTIES, HZ_CUST_ACCOUNTS, HZ_CUST_ACCT_SITES_ALL and HZ_CUST_SITE_USES_ALL, recording each one's primary key and its one foreign key that connects it to the table above it in the identity chain. Then, in your practice environment's Suppliers and Customers work areas, open one real supplier and one real customer record and identify, on screen, where the pay-site/purchasing-site flags and the bill-to/ship-to site uses actually show up.
slots.deliverable: A documented key-and-foreign-key chain for the six supplier/customer/party tables, cross-checked against one real supplier record and one real customer record's site screens in the practice environment.

slots.practicalActivity: Chapter-ending practice for Suppliers and Customers: pick one real party in your practice environment that could plausibly be both a supplier and a customer, and write out how that single party's identity in HZ_PARTIES would relate to a separate POZ_SUPPLIERS role and a separate HZ_CUST_ACCOUNTS role, without duplicating its name or address. Then diagram one customer account with two different sites, each tagged with a different site use (bill-to vs. ship-to).
slots.deliverable: A written same-party dual-role analysis (supplier and customer sharing one HZ_PARTIES identity) plus a diagram of one customer account with bill-to and ship-to sites distinguished.

slots.practicalActivity: Diagram the AP_INVOICES_ALL -> AP_INVOICE_LINES_ALL -> AP_INVOICE_DISTRIBUTIONS_ALL parent/child chain for one invented invoice with two lines, showing exactly which keys repeat at each level. Then diagram the three separate states of that same invoice's payment life -- AP_PAYMENT_SCHEDULES_ALL (planned), AP_INVOICE_PAYMENTS_ALL (applied), and the IBY_ disbursement tables (disbursed) -- marking which state(s) are true right after validation, right after a partial payment, and right after full payment.
slots.deliverable: A header-lines-distributions diagram for one invoice, plus a three-point-in-time diagram showing scheduled/applied/disbursed status at validation, partial payment and full payment.

slots.practicalActivity: Build the mirror-image Receivables diagram: a customer transaction, its receipt, and the application that links them, labeling which table each piece lives in. Then take one real or invented invoice and one real or invented AR transaction and write, for each, what its cached status flag would say versus what you'd need to check to get the actual authoritative remaining balance -- grounded in the lesson's warning that a status flag can read OPEN while the real remaining balance is negligible.
slots.deliverable: A Receivables transaction/receipt/application diagram, plus a written status-flag-versus-authoritative-balance comparison for one AP and one AR example.

slots.practicalActivity: Chapter-ending lab for Payables and Receivables Data: pick one real supplier and one real customer in your practice environment, and for each, build a one-page data map by hand showing every table from this chapter that a transaction for that party would actually touch, from the party's identity through to its payment or receipt status. Annotate each table with its real prefix and primary key.
slots.deliverable: Two one-page hand-built data maps (one supplier-side, one customer-side) tracing a real party's transaction through every relevant table, prefix and primary key annotated.

lessons.title: Following an Accounting Transaction Across Tables
Subledger Accounting Tables and Links to the Ledger

slots.practicalActivity: Diagram the GL_JE_BATCHES -> GL_JE_HEADERS -> GL_JE_LINES hierarchy for one invented journal entry with two lines, labeling JE_SOURCE as either a real subledger value (Payables, Receivables, Assets) or 'Manual.' Then trace PERIOD_NAME across GL_JE_HEADERS, GL_PERIODS and GL_BALANCES for that same journal, and extend the full chain one level further back into the XLA_ Subledger Accounting tables (XLA_EVENTS, XLA_AE_HEADERS) that would have generated it from a subledger transaction.
slots.deliverable: A full traced diagram from one subledger transaction through XLA_ accounting events to a GL_JE_BATCHES/HEADERS/LINES journal entry, with PERIOD_NAME followed through GL_PERIODS and GL_BALANCES.

slots.practicalActivity: Chapter-ending lab for Ledger Data: in your practice environment's General Accounting work area, find one real journal (any JE_SOURCE) and trace it on screen from its batch down to its individual lines and code combinations, then look up its period's status in the period close screens and confirm whether that period is Open, Closed, Permanently Closed, or Future Enterable. Write a short note on what you'd have to do differently if you needed to correct that journal and its period turned out to be Permanently Closed.
slots.deliverable: An on-screen trace of one real journal from batch to lines in the practice environment, its period status confirmed, plus a written correction plan for a permanently-closed period.

lessons.title: Building a Data Map of Your Practice Instance
Data Quality and Common Data Problems

slots.practicalActivity: Starting from the business question "which suppliers have invoices open longer than 30 days" (the course's own example), work through the five-step mapping process by hand: pick the module, identify the 4-6 core tables, trace the keys, note the key columns that matter, and write it down as a short table-by-table glossary of your own. Then list the five recurring data-quality problems (duplicate parties, stuck transactions, mixed entered/accounted amounts, trusted-but-wrong status flags, multi-org bleed) and write one real or invented example of each grounded in tables from this course.
slots.deliverable: A hand-built table-by-table glossary answering the 30-days-overdue question, plus five written examples, one per data-quality problem type, grounded in real tables from this course.

slots.practicalActivity: Course-closing capstone: using only your own data map and glossary from this course (no new lookups), answer in writing which specific tables and columns you would query to find every unpaid supplier invoice over $10,000 that's more than 30 days old -- the exact challenge the next course, SQL for Oracle Financials, will have you actually build in real SQL. Name every table in the chain from supplier identity through invoice to payment schedule, and the one column on each that answers part of the question.
slots.deliverable: A written table-and-column answer to the unpaid-invoices-over-$10,000 question, built entirely from this course's own data map, ready to be turned into real SQL in the next course.

monthlyMilestoneContribution: After this course, a student can read and navigate the real Oracle Fusion Financials data model -- tracing a transaction from party identity through suppliers, customers, invoices, payments, journals and subledger accounting into the General Ledger -- build their own table-and-key data map of a practice instance, and recognize the recurring real-world data-quality problems (duplicate parties, stuck transactions, mixed currency columns, unreliable status flags, multi-org bleed) before they produce a wrong number.
